_: THE SWEEP THAT SAYS THE RECORDER'S CLOCK IS NOT DECORATION — run it from
This round stopped the wrapper `exec`-ing the compiler and made it wait for
one, so that a record could say what the compilation cost. Everything that
buys is downstream and everything it risks is here: a duration that is not
measured, a start that is not a clock, and an exit status that no longer
reaches cargo because a process now stands between them. A green suite says
none of those happened today; it does not say the suite would notice. Each
injection below removes one mechanism and names the test that must go red.
Scoped to this crate's own suite. It has no dependencies and nine tests, so
the whole sweep is seconds — the reason this crate is where the clock lives.

injections.name: the-duration-is-a-constant
injections.why: a wrapper that writes a plausible number instead of measuring one passes every lower bound a test can assert about a compilation, and every second in the census downstream is then fiction — this is the injection the duration assertion alone cannot catch, and the window assertion is what does

injections.name: the-start-is-not-a-clock
injections.why: the start is what joins one wrapper's record to the dozens running beside it, and a zero start makes every job's compiling window begin at the epoch — a span of decades, which reads as a job that was never busy at all

injections.name: the-compilers-exit-code-is-swallowed
injections.why: with `exec` cargo saw the compiler's status because the wrapper WAS the compiler; waiting for it means handing the status over, and a wrapper that reports success for a failed compilation turns every broken build green with nothing else in this repository able to notice

injections.name: a-killed-compiler-exits-zero
injections.why: a `rustc` the kernel kills has no exit code of its own, which is how a runner reports being out of memory; `unwrap_or(0)` is the obvious spelling and it turns the loudest failure a build can have into a pass

injections.name: an-unreadable-clock-reads-as-zero
injections.why: a log written by an older wrapper decodes into perfectly plausible arguments with every compilation costing nothing, and free work is exactly the finding a reader of these logs is hunting for — the tolerant `unwrap_or(0)` is how that arrives as a number nobody questions
